"In yonder groves the happy souls reside,
And in those shades we live, and lie on mossy beds,
By crystal streams, that murmur thro' the meads:
But pass yon easy hill, and thence descend;
The path conducts you to your journey's end."
This said, he led the way, and soon we reached
The hermit's cell, where Vellaisamy prepares
A feast, and bids us welcome to the place.
The modest Gayatri attends her lord,
With every grace of manners, and of mind,
Which women learn from heaven, to practise here;
And Vellaisamy, with looks that speak
His inward virtue, and his open soul,
Proves, by the friendship he to all maintains,
That he deserves the name of great and good.
I saw the pure and mutual confidence,
Which in their looks and actions still was shown,
Of this good couple; and I said within,
Such confidence is the sure guarantee
Of love and constancy. The judge, who saw
My thoughts, approved them, and confirmed my speech,
By his own knowledge of mankind, acquired
From long experience, and a practised eye,
That never errs in judging of the hearts
Of those he converses with. "Trust them," said he,
"For they deserve your trust; and you shall find
Their actions answer to their words, and prove
Their friendship true and constant."'
